case.initial_facts:
A man first developed difficulty organising appointments at age 47. At 49 he had a right parieto-occipital intracerebral haemorrhage, then attributed to hypertension; he recovered physically but required a live-in carer.
By 54, disorientation and loss of recent-event recall had progressed. At approximately 55, speech remained fluent and grammatical, but word retrieval and sentence repetition were markedly impaired; comprehension was relatively preserved. Navigation and dressing also became difficult. He received cadaveric pituitary-derived growth hormone during childhood, including 1974–1985. Current brain imaging, CSF biomarkers, genetic results and pathology are not supplied.

case.hidden: At 56 the patient had advanced disability and imaging abnormalities; later testing and postmortem examination supported high-level Alzheimer-type change with severe cerebral amyloid angiopathy. Those later results and the three other patients’ findings were withheld.
case.reference: Progressive language, cognitive and functional change should not be explained solely by a remote stroke without qualification. Fluent language, impaired repetition and atypical features warrant careful phenotype description rather than a rigid PPA subtype. The childhood exposure is relevant to specialist assessment but does not alone establish the cause in this packet. Neurodegenerative, vascular/mixed and exposure-associated possibilities may be discussed. Pathology, genetic results and current imaging are not established in this packet.
